title: Anthropic reported diary entry to police, woman faces felony charge
content:
What just happened? Another incident has taken place that illustrates the need to be careful what you tell AI. A Florida woman is facing felony charges after she used Claude as a diary and allegedly wrote that she planned to "shoot up" the Sheriff's office. After a human reviewer examined the statements, they were reported to police.
According to the arrest report, Carli Michelle Heller, of Bonita Springs, Florida, wrote on September 26 that she would attack the Sheriff's office. She later said that she uses Anthropic's chatbot like a "diary."
Claude's safety systems flagged the entry and it was escalated to a human reviewer. After deciding it was a credible threat, the reviewer reported it to law enforcement.
The company says it may share user information in limited emergencies if it believes disclosure is necessary to prevent death or serious physical injury.
Deputies identified Heller and visited her home. She was detained without incident before an LCSO intelligence detective took over the investigation.
Heller faces a charge of making a written threat of violence under Florida law. Florida Statute 836.10 makes it a second-degree felony to send, post, or transmit a written or electronic record threatening to kill or injure someone, carry out a mass shooting, or commit an act of terrorism. The communication must be made in a manner in which another person may view it.
Anthropic isn't going to be taking any chances when it comes to anything it deems a potential threat. Last month, it was reported that OpenAI and Sam Altman are being sued by British Columbia over claims that the company could have prevented a mass shooting in the Canadian province.
The shooter, eighteen-year-old former pupil Jesse Van Rootselaar, had previously been flagged by OpenAI's safety team for her conversations about gun violence, but OpenAI never alerted police because the conversations did not meet the threshold for legal referral.
In June, Florida also sued OpenAI and Altman, alleging that ChatGPT had contributed to real-world harms, including the 2025 Florida State University shooting.
The latest incident is another reminder to think before you enter something into a chatbot that could get you into trouble. It's certainly not a private diary whose contents are for your eyes only.
Reports last month revealed that human contractors reviewing Microsoft Copilot's image editor can see users' prompts, uploaded photos and AI-generated edits. Documents show that some of those assignments contain sexual, disturbing or potentially illegal material, though the reviewers are not there to flag the content – only to assess whether the output is accurate.

report.summary: A Florida woman who used Claude as a diary faces a felony charge after Anthropic flagged her alleged threat to shoot a sheriff's office and reported it to police.
report.background: The incident reflects growing tension between AI safety monitoring and user expectations of privacy. Chatbots are often treated as confidential confidants, but their terms allow content to be scanned by automated systems and, in emergencies, reviewed by humans or disclosed to authorities. Claude's safety filters escalated Heller's September 26 entry to a human reviewer, who judged it a credible threat and contacted law enforcement. Anthropic says it may share user information in limited emergencies to prevent death or serious physical injury. The case follows lawsuits against OpenAI and Sam Altman over shootings in British Columbia and Florida, where plaintiffs argue warning signs in ChatGPT conversations should have triggered police referrals. It also comes after reports that Microsoft Copilot contractors can see user prompts and images. Together, these events are forcing the AI industry to confront where safety duties end, where privacy begins, and how consistently threat thresholds should be applied.
key_points: Carli Michelle Heller of Bonita Springs, Florida, allegedly wrote in Claude on September 26 that she would attack the Sheriff's office. She later said she used the chatbot like a diary. Claude's safety systems flagged the entry, a human reviewer deemed it a credible threat, and Anthropic reported it to law enforcement.

Heller faces a charge of making a written threat of violence under Florida Statute 836.10, a second-degree felony. The law covers electronic records threatening to kill, injure, carry out a mass shooting, or commit terrorism if another person may view them.

Anthropic's policy allows it to share user information in limited emergencies when disclosure is necessary to prevent death or serious physical injury. The company applied that exception here. The case shows that AI providers may act as de facto mandatory reporters when conversations suggest imminent violence.

The incident intensifies scrutiny of AI firms' threat-reporting thresholds. OpenAI faces lawsuits in British Columbia and Florida alleging it failed to alert police to warning signs before shootings. Those cases question why one company reports a threat while another does not.

It is also a privacy warning. Reports say Microsoft Copilot human reviewers can see prompts, uploaded images, and generated edits. Users should assume chatbot entries are not private diaries, even if they feel personal, and that flagged content may be read by contractors or reported to authorities.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the case raises the stakes around trust-and-safety operations. Companies must define credible threats, document escalation paths, and balance privacy promises with legal and ethical duties. Inconsistent thresholds across providers could invite regulation or liability. For developers, it highlights the need for robust content-moderation pipelines, human-review protocols, audit logs, and clear user disclosures. It also creates demand for privacy-preserving alternatives. For regular users, the lesson is blunt: chatbot conversations are not confidential. Sensitive journaling, illegal intentions, or anything that could be misread may be stored, reviewed, or reported. Users should avoid sharing incriminating or distressing content with cloud AI and consider local models or encrypted notes when privacy matters most.
report.tools: To keep AI-assisted journaling private, consider local, offline tools such as Ollama, llama.cpp, LM Studio, or GPT4All, which run models on your own hardware. For encrypted note-taking, try Obsidian with encryption, Standard Notes, Joplin, or Cryptomator. Also read Anthropic's usage policies and emergency-disclosure terms, plus OpenAI's safety-reporting guidelines, to understand when providers may contact authorities.
